video.title: How to Count & Inventory Your Draft Beer Kegs

read.bigIdea: What the keg should give, and what it did.
read.where: A half barrel holds **1,984 oz**. Poured as a 16 oz glass with about 1.5 oz of foam (14.5 oz of beer), that’s about **136** pours (Backbar’s method, Level 3). **Yield** is what you actually rang in, in ounces, ÷ what the keg held. If a half barrel rang in **120** of those pours (1,740 oz), yield is about **88%**. Losses add up: Siebel Institute figures **1 oz** lost per pint is **6.25%** of the keg, and every line clean dumps the beer in the line. Track yield **keg by keg**: weighing kegs (Level 3) is more accurate than lifting them.
read.mixup: A keg that “ran out early” didn’t shrink. The missing pours went to foam, spills, comps or pours not rung in.

video.title: Are You Running the Right Pour Cost?

keyPoints.line: moves it without a price change.

read.where: Each beer has its own pour cost (cost ÷ price), but the P&L shows one **blended** number: **all beer cost ÷ all beer sales**. Backbar’s rules of thumb: draft about **20%**, bottles about **25%**. Worked example: **$6,000** of draft at 20% costs **$1,200**; **$2,000** of bottles at 25% costs **$500**; together **$1,700 ÷ $8,000 = 21.25%**. If next month guests buy more bottles and less draft, the blended number **rises** even though no price or cost changed. So read the blend with the **sales mix** beside it.
read.mixup: A rising beer cost isn’t always waste. Check whether the mix shifted toward higher-cost beers first.

video.title: Pour Cost % is a Lie - Track This Instead

read.where: Menu engineering (Kasavana and Smith, Michigan State University, 1982) judges an item by **contribution margin**: **price − cost**, in dollars, and how often it sells. Worked example: a **$6** lager costing **$1.20** is a 20% pour cost and earns **$4.80**; a **$9** Belgian ale costing **$2.70** is a **30%** pour cost and earns **$6.30**. The Belgian looks worse as a percentage but puts **$1.50 more** in the bank per glass. So don’t pull a beer just for its percentage: look at what it **earns** and how often it **sells**.
read.stopsTitle: Two ways to read a beer
read.mixup: The lowest pour cost on the list isn’t automatically the best beer for the business.

read.bigIdea: What should be gone, and what is.
read.where: **Theoretical** usage is what should have left the cooler for what the POS rang in: pours × ounces each. **Actual** usage is the count: **beginning inventory + purchases − ending inventory**. The gap between them is the **variance**. Level 3 taught the formula; here you run it **weekly**, **line by line**, so a gap points to one beer and one week. Small gaps happen; a big one points to over-pouring, foam, unrung comps, a line clean nobody logged, or theft. Write down what you found and what you changed.
read.mixup: Variance isn’t a number to accept. Each week’s gap has a reason; finding it is the job.
